result:
Everyone has a drawer.

It might not literally be a drawer. For some people it's a bowl by the front door, or a shelf in the closet, or that one kitchen cabinet that doesn't really have a purpose. But everyone has a place where things go when they don't have anywhere else to go. In mine there is a single AA battery, dead for at least three years, a tangle of white earbuds where only one side works, three keys that don't open anything I currently own, a takeout menu for a Thai place that closed in 2019, a small blue hair tie, a postage stamp from another country, a USB drive with nothing labeled on it, and a guitar pick even though I don't play guitar.

I have never once looked into that drawer wanting something and found it. That's not what it's for. It's not storage, it's purgatory. It's where objects go to wait while they slowly forget what they were supposed to be.

We lose so much. That should be more astonishing than it is. If you think about all the objects that have ever existed in your life — every pen, every sock, every hairpin, every grocery list scribbled on the back of a receipt — the vast majority of them are gone. You didn't throw them away in some ceremonial way. You didn't give them a proper goodbye. One day you just looked down and your favorite hoodie wasn't in the closet anymore, and you never saw it again. It transitioned from a possession to a memory without any paperwork.

Where do they go? I used to think there was some kind of secret physics to it. When I was a kid, I was convinced there was a place behind the washing machine where socks go to live out their retirement. That felt right. Because socks don't just vanish. They are too humble to vanish. Pens, too. You buy a pack of 30 black ballpoint pens and eighteen months later you own one, and that one is chewed. The other 29 didn't evaporate. So my theory is: they fell through a thin spot.

There are thin spots in every house. The gap between the car seats. The space between the stove and the counter. The top shelf of the closet you can only reach if you stand on your toes. These are borderlands. Objects that roll into them are engaging in a kind of migration. The TV remote that ends up under the couch isn't just lost, it's on an expedition. It wanted to see what's under there. And once it's been under there long enough, surrounded by dust and old Goldfish crackers, it doesn't really want to come back to the bright, demanding world of being used.

But we don't just lose physical things anymore. The modern way to lose something is much cleaner and much more complete. You lose a photo because you switched phones in 2017 and didn't transfer everything. You lose a half-written note because an app updated and logged you out. You lose entire friendships because a messaging platform died and you never got anyone's email. We used to lose things to the junk drawer. Now we lose them to the cloud, which is an even worse drawer because you can't even open it and rummage. It just says "Storage Full" or "File Not Found."

If all the lost text messages and unsent drafts and accidentally deleted voice memos had a physical weight, we would be buried. Every day we produce these huge piles of invisible things and then we misplace them. And yet we still look for them. Have you ever searched your email for a word like "tent" or "receipt" or "love" just to see what comes up from five years ago? It's like doing an archaeological dig in your own life. You find a layer you forgot existed.

Cities lose things too, on a much larger scale. There is a street in my city that used to be a river. They paved over it a hundred years ago, but when it rains really hard, the road still floods in exactly the shape of the old riverbed, because water has a better memory than city planners. Every city has buildings that used to be something else — a church that's now a restaurant, a bank that's now a climbing gym. The old purpose lingers. You can feel it if you sit still enough. The walls remember being something. And there are whole neighborhoods that were once lost on purpose: they changed the name, they re-drew the map, they said this part never mattered. But the people who lived there still tell their kids about it.

The greatest lost-and-found in the world is the ocean. We think of it as empty, but it's just the ultimate junk drawer. Everything we have ever lost eventually wants to go there. Amelia Earhart. The city of Atlantis, if it ever existed. Shipping containers full of rubber ducks from a storm in 1992 that are still washing up on beaches in Alaska. An estimated three million shipwrecks on the seafloor, most of which we will never see. The ocean doesn't organize. It just keeps everything, forever, patiently. It doesn't care if you want it back. It keeps a Lego brick you lost at the beach in 1998 right next to a Roman anchor. It has no system. It is loss without judgment.

This is what I think about when I'm trying to fall asleep, which is most of the time. That we spend so much of our lives trying not to lose things — we put Tile trackers on our keys, we back up our hard drives, we make our kids wear gloves on a string through their coat sleeves — and it doesn't work. Not really. The entropy is too strong. You will lose your favorite mug. You will lose the perfect word that was right on the tip of your tongue in a conversation last Tuesday. You will lose the version of yourself that you were at 19.

And that last one is the hardest, because you can't even prove it was ever there. You tell stories about being a certain kind of person, braver or wilder or more idealistic, but there's no drawer you can open to check if it's true. You just have to trust the inventory of your memory, which is notoriously sloppy.

Maybe that's why we keep the junk drawer at all. Not because we think we'll need that single AA battery someday, but because it's evidence. It's a tiny museum of our own inability to keep track of things, and therefore proof that we lived long enough to accumulate a mess. A perfectly organized house with nothing extra in it looks like no one lives there. A junk drawer looks like someone tried.

I have a friend who, when she moves apartments, unpacks that drawer first. She spreads everything out on the floor of the new kitchen and looks at it and decides what deserves to come with her into the next version of her life. Most of it doesn't make it. She throws most of it away and then, almost immediately, starts a new drawer. Because the point was never the objects.

The point is that we are all, in some way, in the drawer ourselves. Lost, but not truly gone. Waiting to be found by someone reaching in without looking. And most of the time, being lost isn't tragic. Socks are probably happier behind the washing machine. That guitar pick I have never used might finally belong to someone who needs it, if I ever lose it properly.

So if you have lost something recently — your keys, your patience, your sense of direction — just know it's out there somewhere, lodged in a thin spot, keeping company with all the other lost things. They're talking about us, I think, when we're not around. Comparing notes on what kind of people we were when we owned them.
